claim: Impaired spermatogenesis and male infertility are common manifestations associated with mitochondrial diseases.
source: Impaired spermatogenesis and male infertility are common manifestations associated with mitochondrial diseases, yet the underlying mechanisms linking these conditions remain elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about mitochondrial diseases.

claim: PARL-deficient mice are a model of the mitochondrial encephalopathy Leigh syndrome.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that mice deficient for the mitochondrial intra-membrane rhomboid protease PARL, a recently reported model of the mitochondrial encephalopathy Leigh syndrome, develop early testicular atrophy caused by a complete arrest of spermatogenesis during meiotic prophase I, followed by degeneration and death of arrested spermatocytes.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work (Spinazzi et al., 2019) establishing this model.

claim: PARL-deficient mice develop early testicular atrophy caused by a complete arrest of spermatogenesis during meiotic prophase I.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that mice deficient for the mitochondrial intra-membrane rhomboid protease PARL, a recently reported model of the mitochondrial encephalopathy Leigh syndrome, develop early testicular atrophy caused by a complete arrest of spermatogenesis during meiotic prophase I, followed by degeneration and death of arrested spermatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological and immunohistochemical data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Arrested spermatocytes in PARL-deficient mice undergo degeneration and death.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that mice deficient for the mitochondrial intra-membrane rhomboid protease PARL, a recently reported model of the mitochondrial encephalopathy Leigh syndrome, develop early testicular atrophy caused by a complete arrest of spermatogenesis during meiotic prophase I, followed by degeneration and death of arrested spermatocytes.
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations in Figure 2 showing degenerative changes.

claim: The spermatogenesis arrest in PARL-deficient mice is independent of neurodegeneration.
source: This process is independent of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by conditional knockout experiments shown in Figure 1B where nervous system-specific PARL deletion does not affect testicular phenotype.

claim: Genetic modifications of PINK1, PGAM5, and TTC19 fail to reproduce or modify the severe testicular phenotype of PARL deficiency.
source: Interestingly, genetic modifications of PINK1, PGAM5, and TTC19 – three major substrates of PARL with important roles in mitochondrial homeostasis – fail to reproduce or modify this severe phenotype, indicating that the spermatogenic arrest arises from distinct molecular pathways.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis of multiple knockout mouse lines shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The spermatogenic arrest in PARL-deficient mice arises from distinct molecular pathways independent of PINK1, PGAM5, and TTC19.
source: Interestingly, genetic modifications of PINK1, PGAM5, and TTC19 – three major substrates of PARL with important roles in mitochondrial homeostasis – fail to reproduce or modify this severe phenotype, indicating that the spermatogenic arrest arises from distinct molecular pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments showing that modulation of these substrates does not affect the phenotype.

claim: PARL-deficient spermatocytes exhibit severe abnormalities in mitochondrial ultrastructure.
source: We further observed severe abnormalities in mitochondrial ultrastructure in PARL-deficient spermatocytes, along with prominent electron transfer chain defects, disrupted coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis, and metabolic rewiring.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 2C showing swollen mitochondria with irregular cristae.

claim: PARL-deficient spermatocytes have prominent electron transfer chain defects.
source: We further observed severe abnormalities in mitochondrial ultrastructure in PARL-deficient spermatocytes, along with prominent electron transfer chain defects, disrupted coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis, and metabolic rewiring.
evidence: This is supported by blue native gel electrophoresis and respirometry data in Figure 4.

claim: PARL-deficient spermatocytes have disrupted coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis.
source: We further observed severe abnormalities in mitochondrial ultrastructure in PARL-deficient spermatocytes, along with prominent electron transfer chain defects, disrupted coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis, and metabolic rewiring.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HPLC measurements and COQ4 expression analysis in Figure 6.

claim: PARL-deficient spermatocytes undergo metabolic rewiring.
source: We further observed severe abnormalities in mitochondrial ultrastructure in PARL-deficient spermatocytes, along with prominent electron transfer chain defects, disrupted coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis, and metabolic rewiring.
evidence: This is evidenced by increased GLUT1 expression shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mitochondrial defects in PARL-deficient spermatocytes are associated with a germ cell-specific decrease in GPX4 expression.
source: These mitochondrial defects are associated with a germ cell-specific decrease in GPX4 expression leading arrested spermatocytes to ferroptosis – a regulated cell death modality characterized by uncontrolled lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Arrested PARL-deficient spermatocytes undergo ferroptosis.
source: These mitochondrial defects are associated with a germ cell-specific decrease in GPX4 expression leading arrested spermatocytes to ferroptosis – a regulated cell death modality characterized by uncontrolled lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple ferroptosis markers including HNE accumulation, GPX4 loss, and TfR1 overexpression shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death modality characterized by uncontrolled lipid peroxidation.
source: These mitochondrial defects are associated with a germ cell-specific decrease in GPX4 expression leading arrested spermatocytes to ferroptosis – a regulated cell death modality characterized by uncontrolled lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ferroptosis cited from the literature.

claim: Mitochondrial defects induced by PARL depletion act as an initiating trigger for ferroptosis in primary spermatocytes through simultaneous effects on GPX4 and CoQ.
source: Our results suggest that mitochondrial defects induced by PARL depletion act as an initiating trigger for ferroptosis in primary spermatocytes through simultaneous effects on GPX4 and CoQ – two major inhibitors of ferroptosis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the combined data showing both GPX4 loss and CoQ deficiency.

claim: GPX4 and CoQ are two major inhibitors of ferroptosis.
source: Our results suggest that mitochondrial defects induced by PARL depletion act as an initiating trigger for ferroptosis in primary spermatocytes through simultaneous effects on GPX4 and CoQ – two major inhibitors of ferroptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the ferroptosis literature.

claim: Approximately 9% of the global male population is affected by impaired spermatogenesis and consequent infertility.
source: Impaired spermatogenesis and consequent infertility are increasingly prevalent medical concerns affecting approximately 9% of the global male population (Boivin et al., 2009).
evidence: This statistic is cited from Boivin et al., 2009.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of impaired spermatogenesis appear to involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: The underlying mechanisms of these conditions appear to involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, but their specific contribution is poorly characterized (Aitken et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Aitken et al., 2022.

claim: Male infertility has been identified as a significant manifestation of mitochondrial diseases.
source: Furthermore, male infertility has been identified as a significant manifestation of mitochondrial diseases (Martikainen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Martikainen et al., 2017.

claim: The essential roles of mitochondria in reproductive biology, including spermatogenesis, are established.
source: While the essential roles of mitochondria in reproductive biology, including spermatogenesis, are established, their precise mechanisms remain incompletely understood (Cannon et al., 2011; Rajender et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Cannon et al., 2011 and Rajender et al., 2010.

claim: The precise mechanisms by which mitochondria contribute to spermatogenesis remain incompletely understood.
source: While the essential roles of mitochondria in reproductive biology, including spermatogenesis, are established, their precise mechanisms remain incompletely understood (Cannon et al., 2011; Rajender et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Cannon et al., 2011 and Rajender et al., 2010.

claim: Mitochondrial diseases are caused by genetic defects in either mitochondrial or nuclear genome.
source: Mitochondrial diseases encompass a range of inborn errors of metabolism caused by genetic defects in either mitochondrial or nuclear genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial diseases.

claim: The selective vulnerability of specific organs or tissues to mitochondrial genetic defects remains an enigma.
source: The selective vulnerability of specific organs or tissues to these genetic defects remains an enigma and is likely influenced by cell-type-specific activation of poorly understood downstream molecular pathways acting independently of or in parallel with mitochondrial respiratory chain defects.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Energy insufficiency alone cannot fully explain the extremely heterogenous clinical manifestations of mitochondrial diseases.
source: Notably, energy insufficiency alone cannot fully explain the extremely heterogenous clinical manifestations observed (Dogan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Dogan et al., 2014.

claim: Complex molecular responses to mitochondrial dysfunction are gaining recognition as crucial pathogenetic mechanisms.
source: Consequently, complex molecular responses to mitochondrial dysfunction are gaining recognition as crucial pathogenetic mechanisms (Suomalainen and Battersby, 2018; Khan et al., 2017; Forsström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: PARL-deficient mice are a novel model of mitochondrial encephalopathy resembling Leigh syndrome.
source: In our previous study, we described PARL-deficient mice as a novel model of mitochondrial encephalopathy resembling Leigh syndrome (Spinazzi et al., 2019), one of the most common and severe mitochondrial diseases.
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work (Spinazzi et al., 2019).

claim: Leigh syndrome is one of the most common and severe mitochondrial diseases.
source: In our previous study, we described PARL-deficient mice as a novel model of mitochondrial encephalopathy resembling Leigh syndrome (Spinazzi et al., 2019), one of the most common and severe mitochondrial diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Leigh syndrome.

claim: PARL is an evolutionary conserved protease belonging to the rhomboid family.
source: PARL, an evolutionary conserved protease belonging to the rhomboid family, is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and has fundamental roles in cell homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARL.

claim: PARL is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: PARL, an evolutionary conserved protease belonging to the rhomboid family, is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and has fundamental roles in cell homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARL localization.

claim: PARL has fundamental roles in cell homeostasis.
source: PARL, an evolutionary conserved protease belonging to the rhomboid family, is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and has fundamental roles in cell homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARL function.

claim: PARL has been associated with Parkinson's disease, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, and type 2 diabetes.
source: PARL has been associated with various human disorders such as Parkinson's disease, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, and type 2 diabetes, albeit with some controversy (Shi et al., 2011; Hatunic et al., 2009; Istikharah et al., 2013; Spinazzi and De Strooper, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: PINK1 is a substrate of PARL.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Jin et al., 2010.

claim: PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Valente et al., 2004 and Yan et al., 2020.

claim: PGAM5 is a substrate of PARL.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Sekine et al., 2012.

claim: PGAM5 is a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Lu et al., 2014.

claim: TTC19 is a substrate of PARL.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Saita et al., 2017.

claim: TTC19 is a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Saita et al., 2017.

claim: TTC19 is associated with human Leigh syndrome.
source: Notably, PARL's significant role in maintaining mitochondrial fitness has been established through critical studies that identified its substrates, such as PINK1 (Jin et al., 2010), a mitochondrial kinase implicated in Parkinson's disease and mitophagy (Valente et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2020), PGAM5 (Sekine et al., 2012), a mitochondrial phosphatase implicated in Parkinsonism in mice (Lu et al., 2014), and TTC19 (Saita et al., 2017), a mitochondrial protein involved in maintaining complex III activity and associated with human Leigh syndrome (Bottani et al., 2017; Atwal, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Bottani et al., 2017 and Atwal, 2014.

claim: Impaired spermatogenesis is the earliest phenotype observed in PARL-deficient male mice.
source: In this study, we focus on impaired spermatogenesis as the earliest phenotype observed in PARL-deficient male mice, which occurs independently of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on temporal observations.

claim: PARL deficiency leads to a complete arrest of spermatogenesis and triggers ferroptosis specifically in spermatocytes.
source: We find that PARL deficiency leads to severe functional and structural abnormalities in germ cell mitochondria, resulting in a complete arrest of spermatogenesis and triggering ferroptosis specifically in spermatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 1, 2, 7, and 8.

claim: PARL-deficient mice appear clinically normal until around 6 weeks of age.
source: PARL-deficient mice appear clinically normal until around 6 weeks of age, after which they develop a progressive necrotizing encephalomyelopathy resembling Leigh syndrome with death before the age of 8 weeks (Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Spinazzi et al., 2019.

claim: PARL-deficient mice develop a progressive necrotizing encephalomyelopathy resembling Leigh syndrome after 6 weeks of age.
source: PARL-deficient mice appear clinically normal until around 6 weeks of age, after which they develop a progressive necrotizing encephalomyelopathy resembling Leigh syndrome with death before the age of 8 weeks (Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Spinazzi et al., 2019.

claim: PARL-deficient mice die before the age of 8 weeks.
source: PARL-deficient mice appear clinically normal until around 6 weeks of age, after which they develop a progressive necrotizing encephalomyelopathy resembling Leigh syndrome with death before the age of 8 weeks (Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Spinazzi et al., 2019.

claim: PARL-deficient mice exhibit severe testis atrophy.
source: As previously described, these mice exhibit severe testis atrophy (Figure 1A; Spinazzi et al., 2019; Cipolat et al., 2006).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and cited from previous studies.

claim: Cryptorchidism was not observed in PARL-deficient mice.
source: We did not observe cryptorchidism.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the study's observations.

claim: The testis weight of Parl-/- mice at 5 weeks of age is nearly half of that in matched WT littermates.
source: Upon closer examination, the testis weight of Parl-/- mice at 5 weeks of age, when they do not show clinical signs of neurological impairment, is found to be nearly half of that in matched WT littermates (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1A showing statistically significant difference (p<0.0001).

claim: At 5 weeks of age, Parl-/- mice do not show clinical signs of neurological impairment.
source: Upon closer examination, the testis weight of Parl-/- mice at 5 weeks of age, when they do not show clinical signs of neurological impairment, is found to be nearly half of that in matched WT littermates (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The testis weight reduction in Parl-/- mice cannot be explained by concurrent body weight reduction.
source: This difference cannot be explained by concurrent body weight reduction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A where body weight differences are not significant (p=0.0598).

claim: Seminiferous tubules from Parl-/- mice are smaller in diameter compared to WT littermates.
source: Microscopic analysis reveals that the seminiferous tubules from Parl-/- mice are smaller in diameter (Figure 1B; p=0.0002, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and contain approximately 40% fewer cells compared to WT littermates (p=0.0009, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claim: Seminiferous tubules from Parl-/- mice contain approximately 40% fewer cells compared to WT littermates.
source: Microscopic analysis reveals that the seminiferous tubules from Parl-/- mice are smaller in diameter (Figure 1B; p=0.0002, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and contain approximately 40% fewer cells compared to WT littermates (p=0.0009, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with statistical significance.

claim: Seminiferous tubules in Parl-/- mice are populated by immature germ cells exhibiting degenerative changes and prominent intraluminal exfoliation.
source: Further investigation indicates that the seminiferous tubules in Parl-/- mice are populated by immature germ cells exhibiting degenerative changes and prominent intraluminal exfoliation, often in the form of multinucleated syncytia (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in histological images in Figure 1B.

claim: PARL deficiency leads to a complete meiotic prophase I arrest.
source: Immunohistochemistry reveals that PARL deficiency leads to a complete meiotic prophase I arrest as the seminiferous tubules are predominantly populated by SCP-1-positive spermatocytes (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Yang and Wang, 2009; p=0.0001) while spermatids and spermatozoa are completely absent (Figure 1B; Köhler, 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SCP-1 immunohistochemistry in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Seminiferous tubules in Parl-/- mice are predominantly populated by SCP-1-positive spermatocytes.
source: Immunohistochemistry reveals that PARL deficiency leads to a complete meiotic prophase I arrest as the seminiferous tubules are predominantly populated by SCP-1-positive spermatocytes (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Yang and Wang, 2009; p=0.0001) while spermatids and spermatozoa are completely absent (Figure 1B; Köhler, 2007).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 1B.

claim: Spermatids and spermatozoa are completely absent in Parl-/- seminiferous tubules.
source: Immunohistochemistry reveals that PARL deficiency leads to a complete meiotic prophase I arrest as the seminiferous tubules are predominantly populated by SCP-1-positive spermatocytes (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Yang and Wang, 2009; p=0.0001) while spermatids and spermatozoa are completely absent (Figure 1B; Köhler, 2007).
evidence: This is shown by AIF-1 immunohistochemistry in Figure 1B.

claim: The epididymal ducts of Parl-/- mice are smaller in diameter and completely devoid of mature sperm.
source: The epididymal ducts of Parl-/- mice are also smaller in diameter and completely devoid of mature sperm (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in histological images in Figure 1B.

claim: Spermatogonia show a modest increase in number in Parl-/- seminiferous tubules compared to WT littermates.
source: Spermatogonia show a modest increase in number in Parl-/- seminiferous tubules compared to WT littermates (p=0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D with statistical significance.

claim: The analysis of γH2AX expression pattern in Parl-/- seminiferous tubules indicates specific meiotic prophase I arrest at the pachytene stage.
source: Additionally, the analysis of γH2AX expression pattern in Parl-/- seminiferous tubules indicates specific meiotic prophase I arrest at the pachytene stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by γH2AX immunohistochemistry in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Supporting Sertoli cells appear to be slightly increased in number in Parl-/- mice.
source: Supporting Sertoli cells appear to be slightly increased in number (p=0.0382; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F), and the distribution and morphology of Leydig cells appears normal.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E with statistical significance.

claim: The distribution and morphology of Leydig cells appears normal in Parl-/- mice.
source: Supporting Sertoli cells appear to be slightly increased in number (p=0.0382; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F), and the distribution and morphology of Leydig cells appears normal.
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis.

claim: Mice with conditional deletion of Parl in the nervous system (Parl L/L::NesCre) develop severe Leigh-like encephalopathy.
source: To determine whether the observed testicular abnormalities are linked to neurodegeneration, mice with conditional deletion of Parl in the nervous system (Parl L/L::NesCre) were studied. Surprisingly, despite developing severe Leigh-like encephalopathy, these mice exhibit normal testicular size, histology, and sperm production comparable to WT littermates (Figure 1B), demonstrating that the testicular disorder is not a consequence of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the conditional knockout experiments.

claim: Parl L/L::NesCre mice exhibit normal testicular size, histology, and sperm production comparable to WT littermates.
source: To determine whether the observed testicular abnormalities are linked to neurodegeneration, mice with conditional deletion of Parl in the nervous system (Parl L/L::NesCre) were studied. Surprisingly, despite developing severe Leigh-like encephalopathy, these mice exhibit normal testicular size, histology, and sperm production comparable to WT littermates (Figure 1B), demonstrating that the testicular disorder is not a consequence of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The testicular disorder in PARL-deficient mice is not a consequence of neurodegeneration.
source: To determine whether the observed testicular abnormalities are linked to neurodegeneration, mice with conditional deletion of Parl in the nervous system (Parl L/L::NesCre) were studied. Surprisingly, despite developing severe Leigh-like encephalopathy, these mice exhibit normal testicular size, histology, and sperm production comparable to WT littermates (Figure 1B), demonstrating that the testicular disorder is not a consequence of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the conditional knockout experiments showing normal testis despite neurodegeneration.

claim: Nestin (Nes) is expressed in Leydig cells.
source: As previously reported (Anand-Ivell et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2014; Davidoff et al., 2004), Nes is also expressed in Leydig cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cited from previous studies.

claim: Leydig cells are structurally unaffected in the germline Parl-/- testis.
source: Moreover, extensive morphological observations detailed in the following paragraph indicate that Leydig cells are structurally unaffected in the germline Parl-/- testis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the spermatogenetic defect is not secondary to PARL deficiency in these cells.
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The spermatogenetic defect in PARL-deficient mice is not secondary to PARL deficiency in Leydig cells.
source: Moreover, extensive morphological observations detailed in the following paragraph indicate that Leydig cells are structurally unaffected in the germline Parl-/- testis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the spermatogenetic defect is not secondary to PARL deficiency in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal morphology of Leydig cells in Parl-/- mice.

claim: Parl-/- mice exhibit severe vacuolar degeneration of arrested spermatocytes.
source: Conversely, Parl-/- mice exhibit severe vacuolar degeneration of arrested spermatocytes, leading to cell death, and this degeneration progressively worsens from the abluminal to the adluminal compartment (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in electron microscopy and semithin sections in Figure 2.

claim: Degeneration of arrested spermatocytes in Parl-/- mice progressively worsens from the abluminal to the adluminal compartment.
source: Conversely, Parl-/- mice exhibit severe vacuolar degeneration of arrested spermatocytes, leading to cell death, and this degeneration progressively worsens from the abluminal to the adluminal compartment (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: 18.9% of Parl-/- spermatocytes analyzed showed degeneration/death compared to 0% in WT.
source: Analysis of spermatocyte ultrastructure showed a significant increase in the occurrence of degeneration/death in Parl-/- spermatocytes compared to WT (18.9% degenerated spermatocytes out of 201 analyzed in Parl-/- vs. 0% out of 79 WT spermatocytes analyzed; n = 3 for each genotype; p=0.0002 by two-sided Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is quantified from electron microscopy analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Mitochondria of Parl-/- spermatocytes appear consistently swollen with few thin irregular cristae and loss of normal matrix density.
source: Compared to the mitochondria of WT primary spermatocytes, which are typically small with dilated cristae and dense finely granular matrix, mitochondria of Parl-/- spermatocytes appear consistently swollen with few thin irregular cristae and loss of normal matrix density (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 2C.

claim: 92% of analyzed mitochondria in Parl-/- spermatocytes were abnormal compared to 1.9% in WT.
source: Quantitative analysis of the mitochondrial ultrastructure in primary spermatocytes showed a dramatic increase of degenerating mitochondria in Parl-/- compared to WT spermatocytes (92% of analyzed mitochondria in Parl-/- were abnormal vs. 1.9% in WT; n = 3 for each phenotype; p=0.0002 by two-sided Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is quantified from electron microscopy analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Abnormal mitochondrial morphology was the earliest ultrastructural change detected in PARL-deficient spermatocytes.
source: Importantly, abnormal mitochondrial morphology was the earliest ultrastructural change detected in PARL-deficient spermatocytes localized in the abluminal compartment, while adluminal germ cells exhibited additional abnormalities affecting other cell compartments, including the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, and nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Adluminal germ cells in Parl-/- mice exhibit abnormalities affecting the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, and nuclear envelope.
source: Importantly, abnormal mitochondrial morphology was the earliest ultrastructural change detected in PARL-deficient spermatocytes localized in the abluminal compartment, while adluminal germ cells exhibited additional abnormalities affecting other cell compartments, including the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, and nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is shown in electron microscopy images in Figure 2B.

claim: Chromatin clumping and nuclear fragmentation were evident in Parl-/- spermatocytes.
source: Chromatin clumping and nuclear fragmentation were also evident (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in electron microscopy images in Figure 2B.

claim: Spermatogonia, Leydig cells, and Sertoli cells in Parl-/- mice displayed normal ultrastructural features with preserved mitochondrial morphology.
source: In contrast, other cell types within the seminiferous tubules and surrounding interstitium, such as spermatogonia, Leydig, and Sertoli cells, displayed normal ultrastructural features with preserved mitochondrial morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Parl-/- testis mitochondria exhibit remarkable accumulation of uncleaved PINK1 and PGAM5.
source: Parl-/- testis mitochondria exhibit remarkable accumulation of uncleaved PINK1 and PGAM5, as well as almost total lack of the mature form of TTC19 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 3A.

claim: Parl-/- testis mitochondria exhibit almost total lack of the mature form of TTC19.
source: Parl-/- testis mitochondria exhibit remarkable accumulation of uncleaved PINK1 and PGAM5, as well as almost total lack of the mature form of TTC19 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 3A.

claim: The substrate misprocessing findings in Parl-/- testis were consistent with previous observations in the brain.
source: These findings were consistent with previous observations in the brain (Spinazzi et al., 2019) and cultured cells (Saita et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Pink1-/-, Pgam5-/-, and Ttc19-/- mice have normal fertility and testis morphology.
source: In contrast, the single or combined knockouts of Pink1, Pgam5, and Ttc19 resulted in normal fertility and testis morphology, showing orderly and complete spermatogenesis (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by histology in Figure 3B.

claim: The severe testis phenotype resulting from PARL deficiency remained unaltered upon additional deletion of Pink1 or Pgam5 either individually or in combination.
source: Remarkably, the severe testis phenotype resulting from PARL deficiency remained unaltered upon additional deletion of Pink1 or Pgam5 either individually or in combination (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by histology in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of TOMM20 and ATPB were similar between WT and Parl-/- testis.
source: Expression of the outer mitochondrial membrane protein TOMM20 and of the inner membrane ATP synthase beta subunit (ATPB) were similar between WT and Parl-/- testis, suggesting unaltered mitochondrial mass (Figure 4A, Figure 5B, and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figures 4A, 5B, and 6B.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA abundance was not significantly different between WT and Parl-/- testis.
source: Similarly, mitochondrial DNA abundance, often used as an indicator of mitochondrial mass, was not significantly different between the two groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR analysis in Figure 4B (p=0.9146).

claim: TFAM expression did not show any significant difference between WT and Parl-/- SCP-1-positive spermatocytes.
source: Additionally, the expression of TFAM, a protein binding mitochondrial DNA in nucleoids (Ekstrand et al., 2004), did not show any significant difference between WT and Parl-/- SCP-1-positive spermatocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 (p=0.439).

claim: Blue native gel electrophoresis revealed severe assembly alterations in multiple respiratory chain complexes in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
source: Blue native gel electrophoresis revealed severe assembly alterations in multiple respiratory chain complexes, including complex I, complex III, complex IV, and to a lesser extent complex V, as well as the supercomplex (Pérez-Pérez et al., 2016; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Basal mitochondrial respiration in presence of complex I substrates but no ADP (CI LEAK) was significantly increased in Parl-/- testis compared to WT.
source: Basal mitochondrial respiration in presence of complex I substrates but no ADP (CI LEAK) was significantly increased in Parl-/- testis compared to WT, suggesting pathological short-circuit of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This is shown by respirometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: Phosphorylating respiration driven by complex I only (CI OXPHOS) was severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
source: Conversely, both phosphorylating respiration, whether driven by complex I only (CI OXPHOS) or by both complex I and II together (CI + II OXPHOS), and maximal uncoupled respiration, whether driven by complex II (CII ET) or by both complex I and II (CI + II ET) were severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
evidence: This is shown by respirometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: Phosphorylating respiration driven by both complex I and II together (CI + II OXPHOS) was severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
source: Conversely, both phosphorylating respiration, whether driven by complex I only (CI OXPHOS) or by both complex I and II together (CI + II OXPHOS), and maximal uncoupled respiration, whether driven by complex II (CII ET) or by both complex I and II (CI + II ET) were severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
evidence: This is shown by respirometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: Maximal uncoupled respiration driven by complex II (CII ET) was severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
source: Conversely, both phosphorylating respiration, whether driven by complex I only (CI OXPHOS) or by both complex I and II together (CI + II OXPHOS), and maximal uncoupled respiration, whether driven by complex II (CII ET) or by both complex I and II (CI + II ET) were severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
evidence: This is shown by respirometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: Maximal uncoupled respiration driven by both complex I and II (CI + II ET) was severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
source: Conversely, both phosphorylating respiration, whether driven by complex I only (CI OXPHOS) or by both complex I and II together (CI + II OXPHOS), and maximal uncoupled respiration, whether driven by complex II (CII ET) or by both complex I and II (CI + II ET) were severely diminished in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
evidence: This is shown by respirometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: Respiration driven by complex IV was decreased in Parl-/- testis mitochondria.
source: Respiration driven by CIV was also decreased.
evidence: This is shown by respirometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: The respiration defects in Parl-/- testis mitochondria were not attributed to cytochrome c loss due to outer mitochondrial membrane permeabilization.
source: However, the defects were not attributed to cytochrome c loss due to outer mitochondrial membrane permeabilization (Figure 4E; CIV+cytc graph).
evidence: This is shown by the CIV+cytc measurement in Figure 4E.

claim: Cytochrome c-oxidase activity was significantly decreased in PARL-deficient seminiferous tubules but not in Leydig cells.
source: To gain cell-type insights into the observed electron transport defect, cytochrome c-oxidase activity staining was performed on frozen tissue sections. The enzyme function was significantly decreased in PARL-deficient seminiferous tubules but not in Leydig cells, highlighting the specific distribution of the defect (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by cytochrome c oxidase histochemistry in Figure 4F.

claim: COX4 expression was severely decreased in Parl-/- SCP-1-positive spermatocytes.
source: The expression of the subunit 4 of cytochrome c-oxidase, COX4, was indeed severely decreased in Parl-/- SCP-1-positive spermatocytes, confirming the defect in this cell type (Figure 5A; p=0.0027).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 5A with statistical significance.

claim: TOMM20 expression was unmodified by PARL deficiency in SCP-1 spermatocytes.
source: This defect was again unrelated to changes in mitochondrial mass since TOMM20 expression was unmodified by PARL deficiency in SCP-1 spermatocytes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 5B.

claim: Dramatic overexpression of the glucose intracellular transporter GLUT1 was observed in Parl-/- spermatocytes.
source: Interestingly,e dramatic overexpression of the glucose intracellular transporter GLUT1 was observed in Parl-/- spermatocytes suggesting increased glucose utilization as an adaptive response to disrupted OXPHOS (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 5C.

claim: GLUT1 overexpression in Parl-/- spermatocytes suggests increased glucose utilization as an adaptive response to disrupted OXPHOS.
source: Interestingly,e dramatic overexpression of the glucose intracellular transporter GLUT1 was observed in Parl-/- spermatocytes suggesting increased glucose utilization as an adaptive response to disrupted OXPHOS (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GLUT1 overexpression data.

claim: CoQ is a lipid essential for cellular functions, serving both as an electron carrier in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and as a lipophilic antioxidant.
source: CoQ is a lipid essential for cellular functions, serving both as an electron carrier in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and as a lipophilic antioxidant, preventing lipid peroxidation (Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from Gueguen et al., 2021.

claim: CoQ plays a critical role in promoting testicular functions including the maturation of male germ cells by safeguarding against oxidative damage.
source: CoQ plays a critical role in promoting testicular functions including the maturation of male germ cells by safeguarding against oxidative damage (Lin et al., 2021; Mancini and Balercia, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Lin et al., 2021 and Mancini and Balercia, 2011.

claim: Brain mitochondria from PARL-deficient mice have decreased CoQ concentration linked to impaired expression of COQ4.
source: In previous studies, we showed that brain mitochondria from PARL-deficient mice have decreased CoQ concentration linked to impaired expression of the ubiquinone biosynthesis protein COQ4 homolog, mitochondrial COQ4 (Spinazzi et al., 2019), a protein required for the biosynthesis of CoQ (Wang and Hekimi, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work (Spinazzi et al., 2019).

claim: COQ4 is a protein required for the biosynthesis of CoQ.
source: In previous studies, we showed that brain mitochondria from PARL-deficient mice have decreased CoQ concentration linked to impaired expression of the ubiquinone biosynthesis protein COQ4 homolog, mitochondrial COQ4 (Spinazzi et al., 2019), a protein required for the biosynthesis of CoQ (Wang and Hekimi, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Wang and Hekimi, 2019.

claim: An increase in the reduced-to-oxidized CoQ ratio (CoQ red/ox) was observed in neurons due to TTC19 deficiency, leading to complex III dysfunction.
source: Additionally, we observed an increase in the reduced-to-oxidized CoQ ratio (CoQ red/ox) in neurons due to TTC19 deficiency, leading to complex III dysfunction (Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work (Spinazzi et al., 2019).

claim: CoQ levels were significantly decreased in Parl-/- testis.
source: Similarly, we found significantly decreased CoQ levels in Parl-/- testis, accompanied by a dramatic increase in the CoQ red/ox (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by HPLC measurements in Figure 6A (p=0.0001).

claim: CoQ red/ox was dramatically increased in Parl-/- testis.
source: Similarly, we found significantly decreased CoQ levels in Parl-/- testis, accompanied by a dramatic increase in the CoQ red/ox (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by HPLC measurements in Figure 6A (p<0.0001).

claim: The elevation in CoQ reduction in Parl-/- testis can be attributed to impaired CoQH2 oxidation, resulting from compromised complex III activity caused by TTC19 depletion and complex III assembly defects.
source: This elevation in CoQ reduction can be attributed to impaired CoQH2 oxidation, resulting from compromised complex III activity caused by TTC19 depletion (Figure 3A) and complex III assembly defects (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined data from Figures 3A and 4C.

claim: COQ4 levels were substantially decreased in Parl-/- testis.
source: Notably, we also noticed a substantial decrease in COQ4 levels in Parl-/- testis, as seen in the brain (Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry in Figure 6B and C.

claim: COQ4 expression showed a diffuse decrease in various cell types in Parl-/- testis, including germ cells, Leydig cells, and Sertoli cells.
source: Western blotting (Figure 6B) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 6C) revealed a diffuse decrease in COQ4 expression in various cell types, including germ cells, Leydig cells, and Sertoli cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The COQ4 deficit was particularly pronounced in Parl-/- arrested spermatocytes, even those with no or minimal degenerative changes.
source: The deficit was particularly pronounced in Parl-/- arrested spermatocytes, even those with no or minimal degenerative changes, suggesting that the CoQ biosynthesis defect occurred upstream of the degenerative process.
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 6C.

claim: The CoQ biosynthesis defect in Parl-/- spermatocytes occurred upstream of the degenerative process.
source: The deficit was particularly pronounced in Parl-/- arrested spermatocytes, even those with no or minimal degenerative changes, suggesting that the CoQ biosynthesis defect occurred upstream of the degenerative process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that COQ4 is decreased even in non-degenerating cells.

claim: Levels of caspase-3 activation in the seminiferous tubules of Parl-/- mice were comparable to WT.
source: However, levels of caspase-3 activation in the seminiferous tubules of Parl-/- mice were comparable to WT, suggesting that apoptosis was not significantly involved in this phenotype (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by cleaved caspase-3 immunohistochemistry in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apoptosis was not significantly involved in the germ cell death phenotype of Parl-/- mice.
source: However, levels of caspase-3 activation in the seminiferous tubules of Parl-/- mice were comparable to WT, suggesting that apoptosis was not significantly involved in this phenotype (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increased caspase-3 activation.

claim: GPX4 is a crucial antioxidant peroxidase that prevents ferroptosis by reducing phospholipid hydroperoxide in cell membranes using reduced glutathione as substrate.
source: To test this hypothesis, we examined the expression of GPX4, a crucial antioxidant peroxidase that prevents ferroptosis by reducing phospholipid hydroperoxide in cell membranes using reduced glutathione as substrate (Chen et al., 2021; Seibt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Chen et al., 2021 and Seibt et al., 2019.

claim: Immunoblot analysis revealed a nearly complete absence of GPX4 expression in Parl-/- testis.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed a nearly complete absence of GPX4 expression in Parl-/- testis (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 7A.

claim: GPX4 expression was dramatically decreased in Parl-/- arrested spermatocytes but not in Leydig or Sertoli cells.
source: Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence provided cell-type-specific insights, showing a dramatic decrease in GPX4 expression in Parl-/- arrested spermatocytes (Figure 7C, top panels; Figure 8A, p=0.0013) but not in Leydig (Figure 7C, top panels, black arrowheads) or Sertoli cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; p=0.5313).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence in Figures 7C, 8A, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The impact of PARL deficiency on GPX4 expression was not observed in other organs.
source: The impact of PARL deficiency on GPX4 expression was not observed in other organs, indicating a specific effect on spermatocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: GPX4 is not a direct substrate of PARL.
source: To rule out a possible effect of PARL proteolytic activity on GPX4 expression, we checked GPX4 expression in mouse embryonic fibroblasts with and without PARL expression, and knockouts rescued with proteolytically active or inactive PARL. The results do not show evidence of proteolytic misprocessing and do not indicate GPX4 as a direct substrate of PARL (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Parl-/- testis showed significantly higher levels of 4-hydroxynonenal (HNE) adducts compared to WT.
source: Further investigations demonstrated increased lipid peroxidation, as evidenced by significantly higher levels of 4-hydroxynonenal (HNE) adducts, the end-products of lipid peroxidation that defines ferroptosis, in Parl-/- testis (Figure 7B, middle panel), but not in brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 7B (p=0.0199).

claim: HNE adducts were not increased in Parl-/- brain.
source: Further investigations demonstrated increased lipid peroxidation, as evidenced by significantly higher levels of 4-hydroxynonenal (HNE) adducts, the end-products of lipid peroxidation that defines ferroptosis, in Parl-/- testis (Figure 7B, middle panel), but not in brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The accumulation of HNE adducts was particularly prominent in adluminal and exfoliated spermatocytes during the late stages of degeneration.
source: The accumulation of HNE adducts was particularly prominent in adluminal and exfoliated spermatocytes during the late stages of degeneration (Figure 7C, middle panels).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 7C.

claim: HNE signal was dramatically increased in SCP-1 positive Parl-/- spermatocytes.
source: We confirmed these data by quantitative immunofluorescence showing a dramatic increase in HNE signal in SCP-1 positive Parl-/- spermatocytes (Figure 8B; p=0.0002), which is consistent with the specific loss of GPX4 expression in these cells.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 8B with statistical significance.

claim: p53 is a master regulator of both canonical and non-canonical ferroptosis pathways.
source: Additional established biomarkers of ferroptosis, including cellular tumor antigen p53, a master regulator of both canonical and non-canonical ferroptosis pathways (Jiang et al., 2015; Liu and Gu, 2022), and transferrin receptor protein 1 (TfR1), which promotes the cellular uptake of iron via receptor-mediated endocytosis (Feng et al., 2020), were also investigated.
evidence: This is cited from Jiang et al., 2015 and Liu and Gu, 2022.

claim: TfR1 promotes the cellular uptake of iron via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
source: Additional established biomarkers of ferroptosis, including cellular tumor antigen p53, a master regulator of both canonical and non-canonical ferroptosis pathways (Jiang et al., 2015; Liu and Gu, 2022), and transferrin receptor protein 1 (TfR1), which promotes the cellular uptake of iron via receptor-mediated endocytosis (Feng et al., 2020), were also investigated.
evidence: This is cited from Feng et al., 2020.

claim: Excessive intracellular iron can contribute to ferroptosis by triggering lipid peroxidation through Fenton's reaction.
source: Excessive intracellular iron can contribute to ferroptosis by triggering lipid peroxidation through Fenton's reaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ferroptosis mechanisms.

claim: Expression of p53 levels in testis is very low in normal postpubertal mice.
source: In normal postpubertal mice, expression of p53 levels in testis is very low (Beumer et al., 1998) while TfR1 is very high in spermatogonia and gradually decreases during germ cell maturation (Leichtmann-Bardoogo et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2021; Figure 7C, bottom panel).
evidence: This is cited from Beumer et al., 1998.

claim: TfR1 is very high in spermatogonia and gradually decreases during germ cell maturation in normal mice.
source: In normal postpubertal mice, expression of p53 levels in testis is very low (Beumer et al., 1998) while TfR1 is very high in spermatogonia and gradually decreases during germ cell maturation (Leichtmann-Bardoogo et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2021; Figure 7C, bottom panel).
evidence: This is cited from Leichtmann-Bardoogo et al., 2012 and Gao et al., 2021, and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: PARL-deficient testis showed prominent nuclear expression of p53 in adluminal degenerating spermatocytes.
source: In contrast, PARL-deficient testis showed prominent nuclear expression of p53 in adluminal degenerating spermatocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), while TfR1 exhibited persistent overexpression in arrested spermatocytes (Figure 7C, bottom panel), suggesting abnormally high iron uptake.
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: TfR1 exhibited persistent overexpression in arrested Parl-/- spermatocytes.
source: In contrast, PARL-deficient testis showed prominent nuclear expression of p53 in adluminal degenerating spermatocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), while TfR1 exhibited persistent overexpression in arrested spermatocytes (Figure 7C, bottom panel), suggesting abnormally high iron uptake.
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 7C and quantified in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 (p=0.0229).

claim: TfR1 overexpression in Parl-/- spermatocytes suggests abnormally high iron uptake.
source: In contrast, PARL-deficient testis showed prominent nuclear expression of p53 in adluminal degenerating spermatocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), while TfR1 exhibited persistent overexpression in arrested spermatocytes (Figure 7C, bottom panel), suggesting abnormally high iron uptake.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TfR1 overexpression data.

claim: Ferroptosis is a cell-type-specific effect of PARL deficiency.
source: These findings collectively indicate that ferroptosis is a cell-type-specific effect of PARL deficiency and the mechanism underlying the demise of Parl-/- arrested spermatocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ferroptosis markers are specifically elevated in spermatocytes but not other cell types.

claim: Similar spermatogenic defects and neurodegeneration have been reported in Drosophila mutants lacking the mitochondrial rhomboid orthologue Rhomboid-7.
source: Interestingly, similar spermatogenic defects and neurodegeneration have been reported in Drosophila mutants lacking the mitochondrial rhomboid orthologue Rhomboid-7, suggesting that the physiological roles of the mitochondrial rhomboid in these tissues are conserved across different phyla in the animal kingdom (McQuibban et al., 2006; Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from McQuibban et al., 2006 and Spinazzi et al., 2019.

claim: The physiological roles of the mitochondrial rhomboid in testis and nervous system are conserved across different phyla in the animal kingdom.
source: Interestingly, similar spermatogenic defects and neurodegeneration have been reported in Drosophila mutants lacking the mitochondrial rhomboid orthologue Rhomboid-7, suggesting that the physiological roles of the mitochondrial rhomboid in these tissues are conserved across different phyla in the animal kingdom (McQuibban et al., 2006; Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes across species.

claim: Normal spermatogenesis requires a significant metabolic remodeling, with a shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation to support the energy demand for completing the first meiotic division.
source: However, we speculate that these differences may arise from cell-type-specific metabolic requirements. Normal spermatogenesis requires a significant metabolic remodeling, with a shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation to support the energy demand for completing the first meiotic division (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Wang et al., 2022.

claim: PARL-deficient primary spermatocytes are unable to implement oxidative phosphorylation due to their defective respiratory chain.
source: In the absence of PARL, primary spermatocytes seem unable to implement oxidative phosphorylation due to their defective respiratory chain, leading to meiotic arrest, despite compensating with increased intracellular glucose uptake .
evidence: This is inferred from the respiratory chain defects and GLUT1 overexpression data.

claim: The spermatogenesis phenotype in PARL-deficient mice is mainly driven by a germ cell-autonomous defect.
source: These findings suggest that this phenotype is mainly driven by a germ cell-autonomous defect.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-type-specific nature of the defects.

claim: PARL's essential role in cell survival has been established.
source: While PARL's essential role in cell survival has been established (Spinazzi and De Strooper, 2016), its relationship with apoptosis remains contradictory in cellular models (Saita et al., 2017; Cipolat et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Spinazzi and De Strooper, 2016.

claim: PARL's relationship with apoptosis remains contradictory in cellular models.
source: While PARL's essential role in cell survival has been established (Spinazzi and De Strooper, 2016), its relationship with apoptosis remains contradictory in cellular models (Saita et al., 2017; Cipolat et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Saita et al., 2017 and Cipolat et al., 2006.

claim: PARL deficiency induces necrosis rather than apoptosis in the brain.
source: Recent findings indicate that PARL deficiency induces necrosis rather than apoptosis in the brain (Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Spinazzi et al., 2019.

claim: Ferroptosis represents a specific type of regulated cell death, characterized by uncontrolled iron-dependent lipid peroxidation of cell membranes.
source: Ferroptosis represents a specific type of regulated cell death, characterized by uncontrolled iron-dependent lipid peroxidation of cell membranes (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from Chen et al., 2021.

claim: Ferroptosis has been documented in germ cells from Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: While ferroptosis has been documented in germ cells from Caenorhabditis elegans (Perez et al., 2020), it has not been extensively studied in mammalian spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is cited from Perez et al., 2020.

claim: Ferroptosis has not been extensively studied in mammalian spermatogenesis.
source: While ferroptosis has been documented in germ cells from Caenorhabditis elegans (Perez et al., 2020), it has not been extensively studied in mammalian spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Ferroptosis can be experimentally induced in vitro by chemical or genetic inhibition of GPX4, or depletion of its substrate glutathione.
source: Ferroptosis can be experimentally induced in vitro by chemical or genetic inhibition of GPX4, or depletion of its substrate glutathione (Zheng and Conrad, 2020; Stockwell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Zheng and Conrad, 2020 and Stockwell et al., 2017.

claim: GPX4 exists in three distinct isoforms originating from different transcription initiation sites: a full-length mitochondrial form, a shorter cytosolic form, and a nuclear isoform.
source: GPX4 exists in three distinct isoforms originating from different transcription initiation sites: a full-length mitochondrial form, a shorter cytosolic form, and a nuclear isoform (Maiorino et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Maiorino et al., 2003.

claim: GPX4 expression is highest in testis, where the mitochondrial isoform is mainly expressed.
source: GPX4 expression is highest in testis, where the mitochondrial isoform is mainly expressed (Godeas et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from Godeas et al., 1997.

claim: Germline deletion of Gpx4 in mice results in embryonic lethality.
source: Germline deletion of Gpx4 in mice results in embryonic lethality (Yant et al., 2003), while tissue-specific deletions lead to premature death (Seiler et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2021; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Carlson et al., 2016; Wortmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Yant et al., 2003.

claim: Tissue-specific deletions of Gpx4 lead to premature death.
source: Germline deletion of Gpx4 in mice results in embryonic lethality (Yant et al., 2003), while tissue-specific deletions lead to premature death (Seiler et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2021; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Carlson et al., 2016; Wortmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: Spermatocyte-specific Gpx4 deletion in mice causes severe testicular atrophy, reduced spermatogenesis, germ cell death, and infertility.
source: Notably, spermatocyte-specific Gpx4 deletion in mice causes severe testicular atrophy, reduced spermatogenesis, germ cell death, and infertility (Imai et al., 2009), highlighting its importance in male reproductive biology.
evidence: This is cited from Imai et al., 2009.

claim: Reduced GPX4 activity is observed in the sperm of infertile patients.
source: Reduced GPX4 activity is also observed in the sperm of infertile patients, emphasizing its role in human spermatogenesis (Imai et al., 2001; Foresta et al., 2002; Hao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from Imai et al., 2001, Foresta et al., 2002, and Hao et al., 2023.

claim: CoQ provides powerful protection from lipid peroxidation in cell membranes.
source: In addition to GPX4, other defense mechanisms against ferroptosis have been described, including CoQ, which provides powerful protection from lipid peroxidation in cell membranes (Gueguen et al., 2021; Bersuker et al., 2019; Doll et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: The contribution of mitochondria to ferroptosis is still being debated.
source: Although the contribution of mitochondria to ferroptosis is still being debated (Zheng and Conrad, 2020), cumulating evidence indicates that mitochondria are implicated in this process (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Zheng and Conrad, 2020.

claim: Cumulating evidence indicates that mitochondria are implicated in ferroptosis.
source: Although the contribution of mitochondria to ferroptosis is still being debated (Zheng and Conrad, 2020), cumulating evidence indicates that mitochondria are implicated in this process (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Gao et al., 2019.

claim: CoQ is most abundant in mitochondria, where its biosynthesis takes place.
source: CoQ is in fact most abundant in mitochondria, where its biosynthesis takes place, and from which CoQ is then distributed to other cell membranes including the plasma membrane, Golgi apparatus, and endoplasmic reticulum (Gueguen et al., 2021; Stefely and Pagliarini, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Gueguen et al., 2021 and Stefely and Pagliarini, 2017.

claim: DHODH inhibits ferroptosis by reducing CoQ in cancer cells treated with GPX4 inhibitors.
source: Moreover, in cancer cells treated with GPX4 inhibitors to induce ferroptosis, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase DHODH, a mitochondrial inner membrane enzyme involved in pyrimidine biosynthesis, inhibits ferroptosis by reducing CoQ (Mao et al., 2021), suggesting that mitochondrial CoQ reduction inhibits ferroptosis.
evidence: This is cited from Mao et al., 2021.

claim: Mitochondrial CoQ reduction inhibits ferroptosis.
source: Moreover, in cancer cells treated with GPX4 inhibitors to induce ferroptosis, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase DHODH, a mitochondrial inner membrane enzyme involved in pyrimidine biosynthesis, inhibits ferroptosis by reducing CoQ (Mao et al., 2021), suggesting that mitochondrial CoQ reduction inhibits ferroptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the DHODH study.

claim: The lack of GPX4 is per se sufficient to induce ferroptosis in Parl-/- spermatocytes.
source: Although the lack of GPX4 is per se sufficient to induce ferroptosis in Parl-/- spermatocytes, the process appears exacerbated by the concomitant CoQ deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined defects observed.

claim: The ferroptosis process in Parl-/- spermatocytes appears exacerbated by the concomitant CoQ deficiency.
source: Although the lack of GPX4 is per se sufficient to induce ferroptosis in Parl-/- spermatocytes, the process appears exacerbated by the concomitant CoQ deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined defects observed.

claim: PARL-/- cultured cells show increased susceptibility to ferroptosis induction by GPX4 inhibitors.
source: The functional interaction between PARL, GPX4, and CoQ in the determination of ferroptosis is consistent with a recent study, published during the revision of our manuscript, reporting increased susceptibility of PARL-/- cultured cells to ferroptosis induction by GPX4 inhibitors (Deshwal et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from Deshwal et al., 2023.

claim: The mechanism of increased ferroptosis susceptibility in PARL-/- cells involves defective CoQ biosynthesis and intracellular distribution outside mitochondria mediated by the PARL substrate STARD7.
source: The underlying mechanism involved defective CoQ biosynthesis and intracellular distribution outside mitochondria mediated by the PARL substrate STARD7 (Deshwal et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from Deshwal et al., 2023.

claim: GPX4 is not a PARL substrate.
source: Interestingly, GPX4 is not a PARL substrate, hence the mechanism beyond GPX4 loss in this cell type remains currently unclear.
evidence: This is based on the experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: GPX4 deficiency may result from protein degradation linked to chaperon-mediated autophagy.
source: One possibility is that GPX4 deficiency may result from protein degradation linked to chaperon-mediated autophagy, as reported in cells treated with the ferroptosis inducer erastin (Wu et al., 2019), but we cannot rule out a spermatocyte-specific effect on Gpx4 gene expression either.
evidence: This is cited from Wu et al., 2019 as a possible mechanism.

claim: Some interdependence between GPX4 and CoQ is suggested by overlapping inhibitory effects of the ferroptosis inducer FIN56 on both CoQ and GPX4.
source: Interestingly, some interdependence between GPX4 and CoQ is suggested by overlapping inhibitory effects of the ferroptosis inducer FIN56 (Shimada et al., 2016) on both CoQ and GPX4 and by the influence of mevalonate pathway on the isopentenylation of selenocysteine-tRNA (Moosmann and Behl, 2004) needed for efficient GPX4 expression.
evidence: This is cited from Shimada et al., 2016 and Moosmann and Behl, 2004.

claim: GPX4 deficit has been previously found in the brain of CoQ-deficient Coq9R239X mice.
source: Moreover, GPX4 deficit has been previously found in the brain of CoQ-deficient Coq9R239X mice (Luna-Sánchez et al., 2017), suggesting that GPX4 loss and ferroptosis may be an overlooked mechanism of CoQ deficiency deserving further investigations.
evidence: This is cited from Luna-Sánchez et al., 2017.

claim: GPX4 loss and ferroptosis may be an overlooked mechanism of CoQ deficiency.
source: Moreover, GPX4 deficit has been previously found in the brain of CoQ-deficient Coq9R239X mice (Luna-Sánchez et al., 2017), suggesting that GPX4 loss and ferroptosis may be an overlooked mechanism of CoQ deficiency deserving further investigations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation in CoQ-deficient mice.

claim: The distinct vulnerability of spermatocytes to ferroptosis might be influenced by the high poly-unsaturated fatty acid content in these cells.
source: The distinct vulnerability of spermatocytes might also be influenced by the high poly-unsaturated fatty acid content in these cells (Oresti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Oresti et al., 2010 as a possible contributing factor.

claim: High poly-unsaturated fatty acid content could render spermatocytes exceptionally susceptible to lipid peroxidation in the context of CoQ deficiency.
source: This peculiar feature could render spermatocytes exceptionally susceptible to lipid peroxidation in the context of the observed CoQ deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of high PUFA content and CoQ deficiency.

claim: In hearts from mice with mitochondrial genome expression defects, GPX4 expression increases.
source: In hearts from mice with different types of mitochondrial dysfunction, such as mitochondrial genome expression defects (Kühl et al., 2017) or cytochrome c oxidase deficiency (Ahola et al., 2022), GPX4 expression increases.
evidence: This is cited from Kühl et al., 2017.

claim: In hearts from mice with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, GPX4 expression increases.
source: In hearts from mice with different types of mitochondrial dysfunction, such as mitochondrial genome expression defects (Kühl et al., 2017) or cytochrome c oxidase deficiency (Ahola et al., 2022), GPX4 expression increases.
evidence: This is cited from Ahola et al., 2022.

claim: Upregulation of GPX4, sustained by increased glutathione metabolism via the trans-sulphuration pathway and improved selenium incorporation in GPX4, provides a crucial homeostatic response to prevent ferroptosis in heart tissue of Cox10-/- mice.
source: Ahola and collaborators have elegantly shown that upregulation of GPX4, sustained by increased glutathione metabolism via the trans-sulphuration pathway and improved selenium incorporation in GPX4, provides a crucial homeostatic response to prevent ferroptosis in heart tissue of Cox10-/- mice (Ahola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Ahola et al., 2022.

claim: Impairing GPX4 upregulation induced by OXPHOS deficiency through the inhibition of the integrated stress response aggravates the cardiomyopathy of Cox10-/- mice by inducing ferroptosis.
source: Impairing GPX4 upregulation induced by OXPHOS deficiency through the inhibition of the integrated stress response, by knocking out either the mitochondrial protease OMA1 or its substrate DELE1, aggravates the cardiomyopathy of Cox10-/- mice by decreasing GPX4 to WT levels, thus inducing ferroptosis (Ahola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Ahola et al., 2022.

claim: Direct ablation of GPX4 in cultured cells affected by defective OXPHOS induced by a variety of mitochondrial respiratory chain inhibitors is lethal.
source: Moreover, direct ablation of GPX4 in cultured cells affected by defective OXPHOS induced by a variety of mitochondrial respiratory chain inhibitors is lethal (To et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from To et al., 2019.

claim: Prevention of ferroptosis by means of GPX4 upregulation is a required physiological mechanism to prevent cell death in conditions of defective OXPHOS.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that prevention of ferroptosis by means of GPX4 upregulation is a required physiological mechanism to prevent cell death in conditions of defective OXPHOS.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing the importance of GPX4 upregulation.

claim: This study provides in vivo evidence that ferroptosis is spontaneously initiated in PARL-deficient spermatocytes unable to tune up ferroptosis inhibitory pathways in response to OXPHOS deficiency.
source: Our study provides in vivo evidence for this mechanism by showing the opposite situation: ferroptosis is spontaneously initiated in PARL-deficient spermatocytes unable to tune up ferroptosis inhibitory pathways in response to OXPHOS deficiency.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the combined data.
